title: phyloseq
text:
Microbial ecologists usually use the vegan and phyloseq packages to analyse the ASV count data. From the three data tables (taxa, seqtab.nochim, and metadata.data), we will make the phyloseq object ps.

#import your sample metadata
sample.data <- read.csv("sample_metadata.csv")
rownames(sample.data) <- sample.data$sample_names

#check sample names in OTU object
otus <- otu_table(seqtab.nochim, taxa_are_rows=FALSE)
sample_names(otus)

#create a phyloseq object
ps <- phyloseq(otu_table(seqtab.nochim, taxa_are_rows=FALSE), 
               sample_data(sample.data), 
               tax_table(taxa))

#define ASVs
dna <- Biostrings::DNAStringSet(taxa_names(ps))
names(dna) <- taxa_names(ps)
ps <- merge_phyloseq(ps, dna)
taxa_names(ps) <- paste0("ASV", seq(ntaxa(ps)))
ps

#export taxa table from phyloseq
ps_taxa.data <- as.data.frame(taxa(ps))
write.csv(ps_taxa.data,"phyloseq_taxa_table.csv")

#export normalized abundance table
ps_asv_count.data <- as.data.frame(abundances(ps))
write.csv(ps_asv_count.data,"phyloseq_asv_count_table.csv")

#export the fasta sequences associated with your ASVs
refseq(ps)

ps %>%
      refseq() %>%
      Biostrings::writeXStringSet("phyloseq_asv_sequences.fna", append=FALSE,
                                  compress=FALSE, compression_level=NA, format="fasta")

#save your phyloseq object as a .RData 
save(ps,file="ps.RData")

#we can load this object later using the load() function
load("ps.RData")



This phyloseq object - called ‘ps’ - now contains lots of data. We can look at different aspects of that data using some phyloseq functions:

tax_table(ps)
otu_table(ps)
sample_data(ps)

The same way we examined our metadata, taxa table, and ASV table above, we can examine these same attributes in the phyloseq object.
Examining the sample metadata:

#check the first few rows of the data
head(sample_data(ps))

#check the number of samples
dim(sample_data(ps))[1] 

#check the number of variables
dim(sample_data(ps))[2]

#check the numbers of samples per variable
summary(sample_data(ps)$site)

Examining the ASV table:

#check how the raw ASV table looks in the first five rows and first 6 columns
otu_table(ps)[1:5, 1:6]

#check the number of samples (i.e., rows) in the ASV table
nsamples(ps)

#check the number of ASVs (i.e., columns) in the OTU table
ntaxa(ps) 

Examining the taxonomy table:

#check how the raw taxonomy table looks in the first five rows and first 6 columns
tax_table(ps)[1:5, 1:6]





# Convert dataframes to matrices
asv.matrix <- as.matrix(asv.table)
taxon.matrix <- as.matrix(red.taxon)


# Load Phyloseq
physeq <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(asv.matrix, taxa_are_rows = TRUE),
  tax_table(taxon.matrix),
  sample_data(raref.metadat))


#Align sample names in phyloseq with metadata
metadat.physeq <- raref.metadat[sample_names(physeq), ]


identical(taxa_names(physeq), rownames(tax_table(physeq))) # should be TRUE
identical(sample_names(physeq), rownames(metadat.physeq)) # should be TRUE

# Other checks
head(rownames(otu_table(physeq)))
any(is.na(rownames(otu_table(physeq))))
taxa_are_rows(physeq)
any(rownames(otu_table(physeq)) == "")
any(duplicated(rownames(otu_table(physeq))))

title: Introduction to R
text:
Introduction
Being able to work competently with R is incredibly useful and versatile. In addition to performing any statistical tests you like, R allows you to make professional-looking graphs and figures. If there is something you want to do with R, odds are you can do it. You just have to figure out how…
When trying to figure out how to do something, I recommend the following approaches:

Google search what you are trying to do, followed by “in R”. So for instance “Make box plot in R”. There is an extensive user community.
If you see a command in a script you are following, and don’t know what it means, use the ‘?’ function. For example, running ?ggplot will tell you all about the ggplot function, including its available parameters.
Use existing tutorials and resources to give you a pipeline for processing data. Go through with the sample data first to make sure it all works. Then substitute your own data.

Resources I would recommend include:

R for Data Science, Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis, and Advanced R by Hadley Wickham.
Cheatsheets by Posit (formerly RStudio).
Friends Don’t Let Friends Make Bad Graphs by Chenxin Li.
Online R Learning by Chenxlin Li.
The Carpentries workshops e.g., Data Analysis and Visualization in R for Ecologists.
Numerical Ecology in R by Daniel Borcard, Francois Gillet, and Pierre Legendre.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Getting started with RStudio
R is a programming language. In this workshop, we’re going to be working in RStudio, an Integrated Development Environment that lets us easily write and edit code.






RStudio interface
The RStudio user interface has 4 primary panes:

Source pane: allows you to view and edit various code-related files.
Console pane: provides an area to interactively execute code.
Environment pane: displays currently saved R objects.
Output pane: contains the Files, Plots, Packages, and Help tabs.

title: Introduction to R
text:
R basics

Running code
There are a few ways to run code:

Click the line and select CTRL + ENTER
Highlight the line and select CTRL + ENTER
Click the line and click ‘Run’ in the top menu bar
In a R or Quarto markdown document, you can click the green ‘play’ button to run all of the code in the current chunk. Code chunks run from ```{r} to the next ``` . Each chunk should have a unique name.

You can also copy and paste (or type) code directly into the console pane after the ‘>’ prompt. Select ENTER to run the code.


Using functions
To make something happen in R, you use a function. For example, the sqrt function calculates the square root of a given number. To use a function, you’ll need to write it’s name with parentheses.
The inputs you give a function go inside those parentheses - these are called arguments.
For example, we can use the sqrt() function to calculate the square root of 256, by providing that number as our argument.

sqrt(256)

[1] 16


In it’s simplest form, R code works like this:
object <- function(argument)
where:

an object holds a value e.g., the output of a function, a dataframe, a list.
the left arrow operator <- assigns a value.
A function does something e.g., performs a calculation, plots observations.
An argument is an input or parameter e.g., the data or a setting you want to use.



Installing & loading packages


Installing and loading packages
R comes prepackaged with some default functions. You can install packages to get access to new collections of functions.
We can install new packages using the install.packages() function.
We only need to download and install a package once.

#Many popular R packages are hosted on CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network) and can be installed with the install.packages() function
install.packages("tidyverse")

However, every time we open RStudio, we need to load the packages we want to use in that session using the library() function.

library(tidyverse)



Creating objects
If you want to use the output of R functions later, you’ll need to save them. In R, you can save outputs and results by creating an object.
To create an object, type a name for the object and use the <- arrow to store a value in the object. You can call this literally anything you like, so long as it’s one string of characters.

my_favourite_number <- 256
my_favourite_number #this object holds the value '256'

sqrt(my_favourite_number)

my_new_favourite_number <- sqrt(my_favourite_number) #what value is stored in this new object?

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Processing your sequencing reads

Assessing the quality of your .fastq reads
The FASTQ format stores experimental sequence measurements produced by a sequencing instrument. It can be thought of as FASTA, where every base has an associated quality score (hence FASTQ).
A typical single FASTQ read will have four sections:

A header (@) followed by an ID.
The nucleotide sequence.
A header (+) followed by an ID.
The last line encodes the quality scores for the sequences in section 2 (and should be the exact same length).

Below is an example of a high quality FASTQ read. Here, the header line includes a read ID and the length of the sequence.
@SRR1553607.1 1 length=202 
GTTAGCGTTGTTGATCGCGACGCAACAACTGGTAAAGAATCTGGAAGAAGGATATCAGTTCAAACGCTCAAG
+SRR1553607.1 1 length=202
BB@FFFFFHHHHHJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJGHIJJJJJJJJJHHHHHFFFFFEEEEEEEEEDDDDDDDDD
And here a low quality FASTQ read:
@SEQ_ID
GATTTGGGGTTCAAAGCAGTATCGATCAAATAGTAAATCCATTTGTTCAACTCACAGTTT
+SEQ_ID
!''*((((***+))%%%++)(%%%%).1***-+*''))**55CCF>>>>>>CCCCCCC65
Typically, when qualities look like “swearing” in a comic book (!@#$%^&*), it means that the data is low quality.

We can use fastQC to check the quality of our sequencing reads before we proceed with analysis. You can either run fastQC as an application on your computer, or as a tool in the command line. This tool will generate a report that lets us assess the quality of our sequencing data.
FastQC has a really well documented manual page with detailed explanations about every plot in the report. Examples of good and bad fastQC reports can also be found on the project website.


Importing your .fastq files
First we’ll define the path object so it points to the folder containing only the raw sequence read files. Then, we’ll read in the names of the fastq files & perform some string manipulation to get lists of the forward and reverse fastq files in matched order.

#assign path to sequencing .fastq files
path <- "/Users/myname/folder1/subfolder2/MicrobiomeAnalysisWorkshop/fastq"

#check which files are in this directory path
list.files(path)

#read in the names of the fastq files
fnFs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R1_001.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))
fnRs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern="_R2_001.fastq.gz", full.names = TRUE))

#extract sample names, assuming filenames have format: SAMPLENAME_XXX.fastq.gz
sample.names <- sapply(strsplit(basename(fnFs), "_"), `[`, 1)

#check the sample names
sample.names







Considerations for your own data



The string manipulations (which assume a SAMPLENAME_R1_001.fastq.gz file naming convention) may have to be modified if your filename format is different.








Adjustments for iSeq100 (2 x 150 bp) sequences





Read in the forward reads only. For all future steps, only run code for the forward reads.
The iSeq100 processes 2 x 150 base pair (bp) sequences - 1 forward and 1 reverse read, totaling 300 bp. The target sequence length for the 16S rRNA V4 region can vary from 250-350 bp. This means that the forward and reverse reads from the iSeq100 are too short to overlap for V4 sequences longer than 250 bp.
The DADA2 filtering and merging steps requires overlap between the forward and reverse reads to create a full sequence of the target region (16S rRNA V4). This is not possible with the 150 bp reads generated by the iSeq100. Therefore, we can only process the forward read (150 bp). Forward reads are typically higher quality than reverse reads (as you’ll likely see in the read quality profiles below). Although a 150 bp sequence provides less taxonomic resolution than the full 250-350 bp V4 sequence, this is still sufficient to assign taxonomy to our sequences.





Examining read quality
We’ll start by visualizing the quality profiles of the forward reads:

plotQualityProfile(fnFs[1:2])

In gray-scale is a heat map of the frequency of each quality score at each base position. The mean quality score at each position is shown by the green line, and the quartiles of the quality score distribution by the orange lines. The red line shows the scaled proportion of reads that extend to at least that position (this is more useful for other sequencing technologies, as Illumina reads are typically all the same length, hence the flat red line).
The forward reads are good quality. We generally advise trimming the last few nucleotides to avoid less well-controlled errors that can arise there. These quality profiles do not suggest that any additional trimming is needed. We will truncate the forward reads at position 240 (trimming the last 10 nucleotides).
Now we visualize the quality profile of the reverse reads:

plotQualityProfile(fnRs[1:2])

It’s common for Illumina sequencing to produce reverse reads that are of lower quality - especially at the end. This isn’t too worrisome, as DADA2 incorporates quality information into its error model which makes the algorithm robust to lower quality sequence, but trimming as the average qualities crash will improve the algorithm’s sensitivity to rare sequence variants. Based on these profiles, we will truncate the reverse reads at position 160 where the quality distribution crashes.






Considerations for your own data



Your reads must still overlap after truncation in order to merge them later! The tutorial is using 2x250 V4 sequence data, so the forward and reverse reads almost completely overlap and our trimming can be completely guided by the quality scores. If you are using a less-overlapping primer set, like V1-V2 or V3-V4, your truncLen must be large enough to maintain 20 + biological.length.variation nucleotides of overlap between them




Filtering and trimming your data
First, we’ll assign new file names for the filtered .fastq.gz files we’re about to create.

filtFs <- file.path(path, paste0(sample.names, "_F_filt.fastq.gz"))
filtRs <- file.path(path, paste0(sample.names, "_R_filt.fastq.gz"))
names(filtFs) <- sample.names
names(filtRs) <- sample.names

To trim our data, we’ll use standard filtering parameters:

truncLen=c(200,200) : truncLen determines the cut-off length (in base pairs) for the forward and reverse reads.
maxN=0: DADA2 requires reads that have no Ns. This discards any read containing an ambiguous base.
rm.phix=TRUE: PhiX is a small phage originally isolated from E. coli and it’s DNA is commonly spiked in to Illumina sequencing libraries as a control. This parameter removes PhiX control reads.
maxEE=2: The maxEE parameter sets the maximum number of “expected errors” allowed in a read, which is a better filter than simply averaging quality scores. This discards any read with more than two expected errors.
truncQ=2: This truncates a read at the first base with a quality score ≤ 2.
multithread: This should be set to FALSE for Windows Operating Systems, or to TRUE for others.
compress=TRUE: This parameter saves filtered FASTQ files in a compressed (.gz) format.


out <- filterAndTrim(fnFs, filtFs, fnRs, filtRs, truncLen= c(200,200),
                     maxN=0, maxEE=c(2,2), truncQ=2, rm.phix=TRUE,
                     compress=TRUE, multithread=TRUE) #on Windows, set multithread=FALSE

head(out)







Considerations for your own data



The standard filtering parameters are starting points, not set in stone. If you want to speed up downstream computation, consider tightening maxEE. If too few reads are passing the filter, consider relaxing maxEE, perhaps especially on the reverse reads (eg. maxEE=c(2,5)), and reducing the truncLen to remove low quality tails. Remember though, when choosing truncLen for paired-end reads you must maintain overlap after truncation in order to merge them later.
For ITS sequencing, it is usually undesirable to truncate reads to a fixed length due to the large length variation at that locus. That is OK, just leave out truncLen. See the DADA2 ITS workflow for more information.








Adjustments for iSeq100 (2 x 150 bp) sequences






out <- filterAndTrim(fnFs, filtFs, truncLen= 0,
                     maxN=0, maxEE=2, truncQ=2, rm.phix=TRUE,
                    compress=TRUE, multithread=TRUE) #on Windows, set multithread=FALSE (only needed for filterAndTrim)

head(out)

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Denoising
DADA2 attempts to provide the most accurate possible reconstruction of the exact amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) truly present in a sample from the noisy amplicon sequencing reads this process is called denoising. Achieving high accuracy in DADA2 requires both high sensitivity (i.e. reporting as many real ASVs as possible) and specificity (i.e. not reporting out spurious amplicon errors).
Denoising consists of two parts:

Classifying reads as error-free, or not.
Mapping error-containing reads to the appropriate error-free ASV.


Learning the error rates
Every amplicon dataset has a different set of error rates. The learnErrors function estimates the sequencing error rate from your dataset to try and distinguish sequencing errors from true sequence variants (i.e., ASVs).

#learn errors
errF <- learnErrors(filtFs, multithread=TRUE)
errR <- learnErrors(filtRs, multithread=TRUE)

It is always worthwhile (as a sanity check, if nothing else) to visualize the estimated error rates.

plotErrors(errF, nominalQ=TRUE)

The error rates for each possible transition (A→C, A→G, …) are shown. Points are the observed error rates for each consensus quality score. The black line shows the estimated error rates after convergence of the machine-learning algorithm. The red line shows the error rates expected under the nominal definition of the Q-score. The estimated error rates (black line) should be a good fit to the observed rates (points), and the error rates should drop with increased quality.


Inferring sequence variants

#infer real sequence variants (denoised by taking the error rate into account)
dadaFs <- dada(filtFs, err=errF, multithread=TRUE)
dadaRs <- dada(filtRs, err=errR, multithread=TRUE)

#show the results for the first sample's forward and reverse reads
dadaFs[[1]]
dadaRs[[1]]

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Constructing an ASV table

Merging paired reads
This step merges the forward and reverse reads to together obtain the full sequence, based on overlapping regions. By default, this function searches for 12 basepairs that match exactly - this condition can be adjusted using the minOverlap parameter.

#merge paired reads
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaFs, filtFs, dadaRs, filtRs, verbose=TRUE)

#inspect the merger data.frame from the first sample
head(mergers[[1]])







Considerations for your own data



Most of your reads should successfully merge. If that is not the case upstream parameters may need to be revisited: Did you trim away the overlap between your reads?








Adjustments for iSeq100 (2 x 150 bp) sequences






# Merge dadaFs and filtFs
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaFs, filtFs, verbose=TRUE)
head(mergers)










Adjustments for ITS sequencing





For ITS sequences, you should increase the minimum overlap required between the forward and reverse reads, as ITS regions are more variable in length.

#merge paired reads
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaFs, filtFs, dadaRs, filtRs, minOverlap=20, maxMismatch=0, verbose=TRUE)
head(mergers)






Creating the ASV table
We can now construct an ASV table. The sequence table is a matrix with rows corresponding to (and named by) the samples, and columns corresponding to (and named by) the sequence variants.
This step filters out reads with lengths much smaller or larger than our target read length (~250-350 bp). The first step counts the occurrence of different read lengths in a table format. The second step allows you to trim sequence reads that are much shorter or larger than the read length with the highest counts.

#construct ASV sequence table
seqtab <- makeSequenceTable(mergers)
dim(seqtab)

#inspect distribution of sequence lengths
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab))
      
#filter out reads larger or smaller than our target read length
seqtab2 <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 289:296] 
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab2)))







Considerations for your own data



Sequences that are much longer or shorter than expected may be the result of non-specific priming. You can remove non-target-length sequences from your sequence table (eg. seqtab2 <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 250:256]). This is analogous to “cutting a band” out of a gel to get amplicons of the targeted length.








Adjustments for ITS sequencing





For ITS sequences, you should increase the allowed range of sequence lengths due to variability.

#merge paired reads
seqtab2 <- seqtab[,nchar(colnames(seqtab)) %in% 200:500] 






Removing chimeras
Chimeras are not true sequence variants, but rather an artifact of the amplification process. Chimeras are ‘false’ DNA sequences formed by two or more biological sequences incorrectly joined together. Kind of like the mythological creature…

This often occurs during PCR reactions using mixed templates (e.g., environmental samples). Incomplete extensions during PCR allow subsequent PCR cycles to use a partially extended strand to bind to the template of a different, but similar, sequence. This partially extended strand then acts as a primer to extend and form a chimeric sequence. Once created, the chimeric sequence is then further amplified in subsequent cycles. The end result is a PCR artifact that does not represent a sequence that exists in nature.
Chimeric sequences can be identified if they can be exactly reconstructed by combining a left-segment and a right-segment from two more abundant “parent” sequences.

#remove chimeras
seqtab.nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seqtab2, method="consensus", multithread=TRUE, verbose=TRUE)
dim(seqtab.nochim)

#calculate the percentage of sequences that are non-chimeric
sum(seqtab.nochim)/sum(seqtab2)







Considerations for your own data



The frequency of chimeric sequences varies substantially from dataset to dataset, and depends on on factors including experimental procedures and sample complexity.
Most of your reads should remain after chimera removal (it is not uncommon for a majority of sequence variants to be removed though). If most of your reads were removed as chimeric, upstream processing may need to be revisited.
In most cases, this is caused by primer sequences with ambiguous nucleotides that were not removed prior to beginning the DADA2 pipeline. If you see over 25% of your sequencing reads being flagged as chimeric, trim the primers from your sequencing reads and restart the workflow.

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
section: Checkpoint: tracking reads through the pipeline
text:
Checkpoint: tracking reads through the pipeline
As a final check of our progress, we’ll look at the number of reads that made it through each step in the pipeline:

getN <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))
track <- cbind(out, sapply(dadaFs, getN), sapply(dadaRs, getN), sapply(mergers, getN), rowSums(seqtab.nochim))
# If processing a single sample, remove the sapply calls: e.g. replace sapply(dadaFs, getN) with getN(dadaFs)
colnames(track) <- c("input", "filtered", "denoisedF", "denoisedR", "merged", "nonchim")
rownames(track) <- sample.names
head(track)







Considerations for your own data



This is a great place to do a last sanity check. Outside of filtering, there should no step in which a majority of reads are lost. If a majority of reads failed to merge, you may need to revisit the truncLen parameter used in the filtering step and make sure that the truncated reads span your amplicon. If a majority of reads were removed as chimeric, you may need to revisit the removal of primers, as the ambiguous nucleotides in unremoved primers interfere with chimera identification.

Assigning taxonomy

#assign taxonomy
taxa <- assignTaxonomy(seqtab.nochim, "silva_nr99_v138.2_toGenus_trainset.fa.gz", multithread=TRUE) 

head(taxa)

#optionally, we can add species assignments for higher resolution 
taxa <- assignTaxonomy(taxa, "silva_nr99_v138.2_toSpecies_trainset.fa.gz")

head(taxa)







Considerations for your own data



If your reads do not seem to be appropriately assigned, for example lots of your bacterial 16S sequences are being assigned as Eukaryota NA NA NA NA NA, your reads may be in the opposite orientation as the reference database. Tell DADA2 to try the reverse-complement orientation with the argument tryRC=TRUE and see if this fixes the assignments.

title: From raw sequencing data to ASVs
text:
Saving your data
From our ‘raw’ microbiome sequencing data, we have produced the following end products:

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table (seqtab.nochim) which records the numbers of times each exact amplicon sequence variant was observed in each sample.
A taxonomy table (taxa) which records the taxonomic assignments for each ASV.

The most important thing to do at this stage is to save and export our data so we can analyze it later. Today we’ll export these tables to .txt or .csv files.

#make a copy of your final ASV table
asv_count.data <- seqtab.nochim

#replace the column names with ASV numbers
ncol(asv_count.data)
final.asv.names <- paste("ASV",sep = "",rep(1:ncol(asv_count.data)))
colnames(asv_count.data) <- final.asv.names

#export your ASV table to a file
write.table(asv_count.data, file="asv_count_table.txt")

# Export your ASV names (i.e., your taxonomy file) to a file
taxa.data <- cbind(final.asv.names,taxa)
write.table(taxa.data, file = "taxonomy_table.txt")

title: Data viz
text:
Calculating diversity indices
Two common diversity measures reported in microbiome studies are alpha and beta diversity:

Alpha diversity describes the species richness, evenness, or presence alone within a sample.
Beta-diversity measures compare the similarity of two or more communities.


Alpha diversity
Each index take into account different factors which gives them unique advantages for assessing species diversity.

Shannon: based on richness & evenness - prioritizes spread of species within a sample
Chao: based on richness & presence - prioritizes detection of rare species within a sample

Here, we are going to generate alpha-diversity plots following this tutorial.

asv.rich <- estimateR(raref.asv) # calculate species richness - uses integers or counts
asv.even <- diversity(asv.table) / log(specnumber(asv.table)) # calculate species evenness - uses proportion

# Calculate diversity index that combines species richness and evenness
asv.div <- diversity(asv.table, index="shannon") # replace with chao or simpson

hist(asv.div, main = "Histogram of Shannon Diversity", xlab = "Shannon Diversity")

# Test normality of distribution
shapiro.test(asv.div) # <0.01 is non-normal

# Plot with statistical test by treatment (e.g. by Steep_Time)
common <- intersect(names(asv.div), rownames(asv.table))

df.shannon <- data.frame(
  Shannon = asv.div[common],
  Steep_Time = raref.metadat[common, "Steep_Time"]
)


df.shannon$Steep_Time <- factor(df.shannon$Steep_Time, 
                              levels = c("0", "1", "2", "5", "14", "21", "28"))

# Test statistical significance between diversity indices of each treatment level
kruskal.test(Shannon ~ Steep_Time, data = df.shannon) # Kruskal-Wallis is a statistical test for non-normal distributions

pairwise.wilcox.test(df.shannon$Shannon, df.shannon$Steep_Time,
                     p.adjust.method = "fdr") # p-adjusment helps limit false positives from multiple comparisons

quartz() # opens a new figure window on Mac
ggplot(df.shannon, aes(x = Steep_Time, y = Shannon, fill = Steep_Time)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, size = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Shannon Diversity over Time spent in Compost Tea",
       x = "Steep Time",
       y = "Shannon Diversity") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("28" = "#006475", "21" = "#00a1b7", "14" = "#56d0d8", "5" = "#596028", "2" = "#898929", "1"="#606571", "0" = "black")) +
  stat_compare_means(method = "kruskal.test", label.y = max(df.shannon$Shannon) + 0.7) +
  stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test",
                     comparisons = list(c("0", "1", "2", "5", "14", "21", "28")),
                    label = "p.signif")







Considerations for your own data



Using bullet points, write down everything you notice about the plots you produced.
What do you understand? What do you find confusing?
If you were going to publish these plots in a scientific paper, what features would you want to improve or add?
Now try plotting and running a statstical comparison for another variable. Adjust the necessary parameters and objects from the code above to assess a new variable’s levels. Which do you think may have the strongest impact on the final microbiome composition?




Beta diversity

Principal Components Analysis (PCoA)
A Principals Component Analysis, or PCoA, is an ordination technique that lets us visualize high-dimensional data. In a nutshell, it reduces high-dimensional data into a smaller number of dimensions so we can plot it in 2D.

asv.bray <- vegdist(asv.table)

asv.bray.table <- as.data.frame(asv.bray)


asv.pcoa <- cmdscale(asv.bray, k=(nrow(asv.perc)-1), eig=TRUE)

# Store coordinates for first two axes in new variable #
asv.p <- asv.pcoa$points[,1:2]

# Calculate % variance explained by each axis #
asv.eig<-asv.pcoa$eig
perc.exp<-asv.eig/(sum(asv.eig))*100
pe1<-perc.exp[1]
pe2<-perc.exp[2]

# Build PCoA dataframe
pcoa_df <- data.frame(
  Sample = rownames(asv.p),
  PCoA1 = asv.p[,1],
  PCoA2 = asv.p[,2],
  Group = raref.metadat$Steep_Time)

ggplot(pcoa_df, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, color = Group, fill = Group)) +
 geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3, stroke = 1) +
  labs(x = paste0("PCoA1 (", round(pe1, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", round(pe2, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    title = "PCoA of ASVs (Bray-Curtis)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c( "1" = "gray", "2" = "red", "5" = "orange", "14" = "gold", "21" = "chartreuse4","28" = "blue1"), breaks = c("1", "2", "5", "14", "21", "28")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c( "1" = "gray", "2" = "red", "5" = "orange", "14" = "gold", "21" = "chartreuse4","28" = "blue1"), breaks = c("1", "2", "5", "14", "21", "28")) + 
  theme_minimal()

You can play with removing points from the plot to see how treatment groups may be separating from each other. However, this is not a true subset.

pcoa_df_sub <- subset(pcoa_df, Group %in% c("1", "28"))

ggplot(pcoa_df_sub, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, color = Group, fill = Group)) +
 geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3, stroke = 1) +
  labs(x = paste0("PCoA1 (", round(pe1, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", round(pe2, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    title = "PCoA of ASVs (Bray-Curtis)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c( "1" = "gray", "28" = "blue1"), breaks = c("1", "28")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c( "1" = "gray", "28" = "blue1"), breaks = c("1", "28")) + 
  theme_minimal()

If you want to run an analysis on a subset of your data, you must re-calculate the diversity index. This will now replace the objects you created previously. Notice how this changes the % vairance explained.

# Beta diversity index
asv.bray <- vegdist(asv.Day1.28)
asv.bray.table <- as.data.frame(asv.bray)

asv.pcoa <- cmdscale(asv.bray, k=(nrow(asv.Day1.28)-1), eig=TRUE)

# Store coordinates for first two axes in new variable #
asv.p <- asv.pcoa$points[,1:2]

# Calculate % variance explained by each axis #
asv.eig<-asv.pcoa$eig
perc.exp<-asv.eig/(sum(asv.eig))*100
pe1<-perc.exp[1]
pe2<-perc.exp[2]

pcoa_df_sub <- subset(pcoa_df, Group %in% c("1", "28"))

ggplot(pcoa_df_sub, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, color = Group, fill = Group)) +
 geom_point(shape = 21, size = 3, stroke = 1) +
  labs(x = paste0("PCoA1 (", round(pe1, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", round(pe2, 2), "% variance explained)"),
    title = "PCoA of ASVs (Bray-Curtis)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c( "1" = "gray", "28" = "blue1"), breaks = c("1", "28")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c( "1" = "gray", "28" = "blue1"), breaks = c("1", "28")) + 
  theme_minimal()

text:
In this session, we will: - Examine these data tables. - Perform necessary quality control checks (e.g., sparsity and sequencing depth). - Filter & normalize our data by sample.
So far, we have created two data tables using the DADA2 pipeline:

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table (asv_count.data) which records the numbers of times each exact amplicon sequence variant was observed in each sample.
A taxonomy table (taxa.data) which records the taxonomic assignments for each ASV.

We’ll also be working with a metadata table (sample.data) which represents metadata information for the different samples.


By the end of today’s session, you should be able to:

Interpret multidimensional data from genomic sequencing and how to successfully align all features for microbiome analysis
Examine typical aspects of microbiome genomic sequence output and critically evaluate the quality
Apply key data manipulation steps and determine when each is appropriate
Evaluate experimental hypotheses through data summary and subsetting





library(tidyverse)
library(phyloseq)

#import our asv and taxa tables
asv_count.data <- read.table(file="asv_count_table.txt", sep = " ", header = TRUE, quote = "\"", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

taxa.data <- read.table(file = "taxonomy_table.txt"), sep = " ", header = TRUE, quote = "\"", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

sample.data <- read.csv("sample_metadata.csv")





#check the first few rows of the data
head(metadata.data)

#check the number of samples
dim(metadata.data)[1]

#check the number of variables
dim(metadata.data)[2] 

#check the numbers of samples per variable
summary(metadata.data)







Discussion point



Most datasets will have have multiple variables with an underlying experimental design. What would be your first idea to analyze this data?





The taxonomy table (taxa.data) represents the assignment for the different ASVs at domain, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species levels.



#check the first few rows of the data
head(taxa.data)
taxa.data[1:5, 1:6]

#check the number of x
dim(taxa.data)[1]

#check the number of y
dim(taxa.data)[2] 

#check the numbers of samples per variable
summary(taxa.data)




From our ‘raw’ taxonomy table (taxa.data), we are going to explicitly define ASVs with no taxonomy data as “unclassified”.

#check the first few rows of the data
head(taxa.data)

#set the ASV IDs as row names
rownames(taxa.data) <- taxa.data[,1] 

#what does this do?
taxa.data <- taxa.data[,-c(1,1)]

#classify ASVs without any taxonomy data as "unclassified"
taxa.data[taxa.data == "" | is.na(taxa.data)] <- "unclassified"

Next, we will remove unwanted classifications or ASVs. This includes:

Unclassified sequences (with no taxonomy data).
Archaeal sequences.
Mitochondrial sequence contamination.
Chloroplastic sequence contamination (particularly when sampling microbiomes associated with plants).

unclassified.ASVs <- subset(taxa.data, Phylum == "unclassified")
#check the first few rows of the data
head(unclassified.taxa)

#defining a list of archaeal ASVs
archaea.ASVs <- subset(taxa.data, Kingdom == "Archaea")

) %>% reduce(union)

ASVs_to_remove

#check the number of y
dim(filtered_taxa.data)[2] 

#check the numbers of samples per variable
summary(filtered_taxa.data)





The ASV table (asv_count.data) is the abundance table that contains counts corresponding to the number of times each ASV is observed in each sample.


The ASV table has samples in rows and variables (ASVs) in columns.
Check the first few rows of the ASV table:

#check how the raw ASV table looks in the first five rows and first 6 columns
asv_count.data[1:5, 1:6]

Check the total number of reads:

#check the total number of sequences/reads in the ASV table
sum(asv_count.data)

Check the number of samples & ASVs:

#check the number of samples (i.e., rows) in the ASV table
dim(asv_count.data)[1] 

#check the number of ASVs (i.e., columns) in the OTU table
dim(asv_count.data)[2]




We have already filtered out unwanted classifications and ASVs from the taxonomy table to create filtered_taxa.data. Next, we’ll update the ASV table to match by remvoving the same unwanted ASVs.

#keep ASV columns from the ASV table that match the row names in the filtered taxa table
filtered_asv_count.data <- asv_count.data[,which(colnames(asv_count.data) %in% rownames(filtered_taxa.data))]

Check the dimensions of the filtered taxonomy table:

#check the first few rows of the data
head(filtered_asv_count.data)

#check the total number of sequences/reads in the ASV table
sum(filtered_asv_count.data)

#check the number of samples (i.e., rows) in the ASV table
dim(filtered_asv_count.data)[1] 

#check the number of ASVs (i.e., columns) in the ASV table
dim(filtered_asv_count.data)[2]

#check the numbers of samples per variable
summary(filtered_asv_count.data)




Microbiome datasets are usually sparse and have an uneven library size.
Check the number of zeros & percentage of zeros in the ASV table:

#check the number of zeros in the ASV table
sum(filtered_asv_count.data == 0)

#check the percentage of zeros in the ASV table
sum(filtered_asv_count.data == 0) / (nb_var * nb_samples) * 100







Discussion point




What is the meaning of a zero value in an ASV table?
Can we consider it to be a true zero?
Do you think it is important to filter the data and why?









Answers






A zero value in the ASV table means that we could not sequence any read for a specific ASV in a given sample. This means that the ASV is not present in the given sample, or that the sequencing depth was not enough to find it.
Because of this, we usually don’t know if it is a true zero or not.
The issue of whether something is truly absent (or not) is problematic, especially when we have to compare rare ASVs. Furthermore, some statistical approaches cannot handle highly sparse data set (e.g., Principal Component Analysis). For microbiome data analysis, zeros values can be difficult to analyse and interpret and data should be filtered if the percentage of zeros is relatively high.










Considerations for your own data




Microbial ecologists usually remove singletons (ASVs for which only one read has been identified in the full ASV table), as these are likely to be artifacts.
Another option for data filtering could be to remove ASVs that have a total count (per ASV, over all samples) lower than a defined value.
As a reminder, chimeric amplification products have been already removed in DADA2 pipeline.



Plot the ASV occurrence frequency as a histogram:

hist(as.matrix(filtered_asv_count.data), 
     max(filtered_asv_count.data), 
     right = FALSE, 
     las = 1, 
     xlab = "Occurrence value", 
     ylab = "Frequency", 
     main = "Occurrence frequency")

There will likely be a lot of low occurrences (such as 0, 1, or 2 counts per ASV and per sample) and few abundant ASVs.
Get the minimum total ASV count over all samples:

min(colSums(filtered_asv_count.data))

Check how frequently ASVs are shared between samples:

non_zero <- 0*1:nb_var

for (i in 1:nb_var){
  non_zero[i]<-sum(filtered_asv_count.data[,i] != 0)
  }

plot(non_zero, xlab = "ASV", ylab = "Frequency", main = "Number of non zero values", las = 1)

It is likely that the majority of ASVs are found only in a few samples. In other words, very few ASVs will be found at high frequencies or across all samples.






Considerations for your own data



If you have replicate samples, you could think about filtering out rare ASVs that are not shared between at least 2 or 3 samples.





Sequencing depth and library size represent the number of counts per sample. This number can vary a lot among the different samples (up to 10-fold).
Differences in library size can be due to technical biases or errors introduced when creating DNA sequencing libraries in the lab: - The PCR amplification step can introduce some difference among samples because PCR amplification can be more orless efficient according to the sequence itself. - After cleaning up PCR amplicons from each sample, we typically measure the DNA concentration. Depending on the method used (e.g., band brightness, NanoDrop, Qubit), this may not be a highly accurate or sensitive measure. - Then, according to these concentrations, we pool the different samples into one ‘equimolar’ mix, which can also introduce some error.






Discussion point



Why do you think it is important to look at sequencing depth?








Answers






It is important to know if we sequenced enough to capture all the diversity present in our environment.
To compare samples to each other, we need to have a comparable library size between samples.







Check the number of ASV counts per sample:

#calculate the number of counts per sample
library_size <- rowSums(filtered_asv_count.data)
summary(library_size)

#check if any samples have zero counts
library_size[library_size == 0]

#plot the number of counts per sample as a histogram
plot(library_size, ylim=c(0,25000), main=c("Number of counts per sample"), xlab=c("Samples"))

#check the minimum library size
min(library_size)

#check the maximum library size
max(library_size)







Considerations for your own data



Do your samples have differences in the library size? If you want to compare samples to each other (hint: you do), it will be an issue to have different library sizes. To fix this, we will normalize our library sizes.
If any of your samples have no counts at all, they should be removed from analysis.

text:
Normalizing abundance data

Checking the rarefaction curve
We can explore sequencing depth though a rarefaction curve. The rarefaction curve shows how many new ASVs are observed when we obtain new reads for a given sample - essentially visualizing ASV richness across sampling depths.

rarecurve(filtered_asv_count.data, step = 100, cex = 0.75, las = 1, xlab="Number of reads", ylab = "Number of ASVs observed") 

The key to interpreting these curves is to identify where ASV richness plateaus. If the sequencing depth is sufficient, we should observe a plateau. This means that even if we sequence new reads from that sample, they will belong to ASVs already observed. In other word, all the diversity present in a sample is already captured and we have sequenced the community deeply enough.
The sequencing depth at which ASV richness plateaus can serve as the cut-of point for normalization. This allows us to retain the maximum amount of ASV diversity, while creating even sequence depth across samples for downstream processing. Rarefying is ideal for beta diversity analyses.






Considerations for your own data



Do your samples reach a plateau? Does the total number of reads vary between samples?

From our ‘raw’ data tables, we have produced the following end products:

An amplicon sequence variant (ASV) count table (asv_relative_abundance.data) which has:

Been filtered to remove unwanted ASVs
Been normalized to rarefy samples
Had counts converted to relative abundance (%)

A taxonomy table (filtered_taxa.data) which records the taxonomic assignments for each ASV which has:

Been filtered to remove unwanted ASVs

Negative controls
It is important to include negative controls throughout the extraction and amplification process. These can include blank samples that go through the extraction process, and no-template controls that go through the amplification process. These negatives can then be used to ensure these steps are not amplifying unwanted DNA from the laboratory environment

Scroll to BLANK or NEG samples
Order from high to low to see counts for most abundant ASVs
Interpret:


Reads should be below 1000 per ASV
Sample should contain less than 100 different ASVs
If higher than these benchmarks, this could be problematic for interpreting ASVs in actual samples and further steps should be taken to account for these ASVs
